title:
Nested Instrumental Variables Design: Switcher Average Treatment Effect,
  Identification, Efficient Estimation and Generalizability

sections.text:
#### Abstract

Instrumental variables (IV) are a commonly used tool to estimate causal effects from nonrandomized data. An archetype of an IV is a randomized trial with non-compliance where the randomized treatment assignment serves as an IV for the non-ignorable treatment received. Under a monotonicity assumption, a valid IV non-parametrically identifies the average treatment effect among a non-identified, latent complier subgroup, whose generalizability is often under debate. In many studies, there could exist multiple versions of an IV, for instance, different nudges to take the same treatment in different study sites in a multicentre clinical trial. These different versions of an IV may result in different compliance rates and offer a unique opportunity to study IV estimates' generalizability. In this article, we introduce a novel nested IV assumption and study identification of the average treatment effect among two latent subgroups: always-compliers and switchers, who are defined based on the joint potential treatment received under two versions of a binary IV. We derive the efficient influence function for the SWitcher Average Treatment Effect (SWATE) under a non-parametric model and propose efficient estimators. We then propose formal statistical tests of the generalizability of IV estimates under the nested IV framework. We apply the proposed method to the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial and study the causal effect of colorectal cancer screening and its generalizability. # 1 Introduction
### 1.1 Instrumental variable (IV); complier average treatment effect; generalizability

Scientific inquiries often involve investigating cause-and-effect relationships. Randomization is a powerful tool for drawing valid causal inference. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are widely regarded as the gold standard for establishing causality. However, drawing a valid causal conclusion from non-randomized studies is often challenging due to many factors, unmeasured confounding being a primary concern. To address the potential bias introduced by unmeasured confounders, researchers often turn to quasi-experimental methods (Cook et al., 1979), with instrumental variable (IV) methods being among the most widely used approaches (Angrist et al., 1996; Hernán and Robins, 2006; Baiocchi et al., 2014). A variable is a valid IV if it is correlated with the treatment, does not have a direct effect on the outcome under investigation and is independent of unmeasured treatment-outcome confounders (see, e.g., Baiocchi et al., 2014). Econometricians popularized IV methods under the framework of linear structural equations with omitted variables (see, e.g., Goldberger, 1972). Angrist et al. (1996) first formalized an IV under the potential outcomes (PO) framework (Neyman, 1923; Rubin, 1974), defined the complier average treatment effect (CATE) as a key estimand and studied its non-parametric identification under a monotonicity assumption which states that the level of a person's treatment received cannot decrease as the level of IV increases. The concept of identifying and estimating causal effects among a latent subpopulation defined by potential outcomes under both treatment assignments (referred to as "cross-world" potential outcomes) was referred to as principal stratification and later generalized to other contexts, including surrogate endpoints, truncation by death, among others (Frangakis and Rubin, 2002; Zhang and Rubin, 2003; Gilbert and Hudgens, 2008).

A key critique towards the CATE framework, and principal stratification in general, is that the CATE only concerns the causal effect of a latent subgroup and cannot be generalized to the entire population without further assumptions; see, e.g., the extensive discussion in Deaton (2009), Heckman and Urzua (2010), Joffe (2011), among others. One strand of work seeks to illuminate the relationship between the CATE and the average treatment effect (ATE) or the av-

erage treatment effect on the treated (ATT) by proposing suitable identification assumptions that point identify the ATE with a valid IV. These assumptions typically impose some homogeneity or no-interaction-type restrictions on the data generating processes (Swanson et al., 2018; Levis et al., 2024). For instance, with a binary IV and a binary treatment, Robins (1994) proposed the no-current-treatment-interaction assumption, which states that there is no additive interaction between the IV and treatment in the model for conditional average treatment effect. An alternative assumption is the homogeneous selection bias assumption proposed by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Vansteelandt (2013), which posits that the selection bias function is independent of the value of the IV on an additive scale and identifies the ATT using a valid IV. More recently, Wang and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2018) showed that if there is no additive unmeasured confounder-IV interaction in the model for treatment or additive unmeasured confounder-treatment interaction in the model for potential outcomes, then the ATE can be identified by an IV. These assumptions are typically not empirically verifiable and are scale-specific (i.e., only suitable for an additive or multiplicative scale). Under the principal stratification framework, a similar assumption called principal ignorability, which states that there is no difference in the average potential outcomes across principal strata conditional on baseline covariates, is needed for generalizability (Jo and Stuart, 2009). Unfortunately, the principal ignorability assumption is also not empirically verifiable.

# 1.2 A clinical trial with two versions of an IV; nested IV 

The archetype of an IV is an RCT with non-compliance, where the treatment assignment serves as a randomized encouragement to receive the treatment, thereby acting as an IV for the actual treatment uptake. The Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial is a multiphasic RCT conducted from 1993 to 2011 at 10 US institutions. A total of 154,897 participants, aged 55 to 74 years, were enrolled and randomized to either the intervention or control arm. Participants in the intervention arm were offered cancer screening exams, while those in the control arm were advised to receive their usual medical care.

Two methods of consent were used in this trial. Seven centres employed a single consent process, while the remaining three initially adopted a dual consent process. In centres using the single consent process, enrollment and randomization were consented to simultaneously. In centres using the dual consent process, participants were not informed of the study design, including the

type of intervention, during the initial enrollment and first consent. Later, participants randomized to the intervention arm were informed of their treatment assignment and asked to consent again for the administration of the intervention. The results indicated that the overall compliance rate among participants in the single consent process was $91.3 \%$, while the compliance rate among participants in the dual consent process dropped to $71.2 \%$. Due to the high rate of refusal to receive the screening intervention among dual-consent participants, the three screening centres later switched to the single consent process. In a post hoc analysis, Marcus et al. (2014) found that the single versus dual consent process was significantly associated with receiving the cancer screening (odds ratio $=2.2 ; 95 \%$ CI: 2.0 to 2.5 ), even after adjusting for a comprehensive set of baseline characteristics, including age at randomization, race and ethnicity, gender, education, BMI, comorbidity score, and others.

The transition from single to dual consent process created a natural experiment that strengthened the encouragement to comply with the treatment assignment. Given Marcus et al.'s (2014) analysis, it is not unreasonable to assume that a complier under the dual consent process would remain a complier had the person enrolled in the study during the single consent stage. We will refer to the assumption that a complier under one binary IV would remain a complier under a second, strengthened IV as a "nested IV" assumption. In addition to being induced by a sudden policy shift like that in the PLCO trial, multiple versions of an IV, possibly with varying strength, are prevalent in modern-day trials:

1. Multicentre trials. Contemporary multicentre clinical trials often involve a large number of investigative centres in order to recruit a large number of study participants. In multicentre trials, non-compliance was often variable among different investigative centres. The randomization scheme at each centre can be viewed as a different version of an IV.
2. Integrative/Meta-analysis of multiple trials. Compliance rates often vary across different clinical trials investigating the same intervention. For instance, Zhou et al. (2019, Figure 1) summarizes the study-specific compliance rates in 10 studies of epidural analgesia, with rates ranging from less than $5 \%$ to over $50 \%$ across these studies. As another example, in different trials testing the same HIV prevention modality (e.g., daily oral prophylaxis) in similar study populations (e.g., heterosexual women in sub-Saharan Africa), compliance rates

varied due to a variety of factors (Cohen and Baden, 2012; He et al., 2023), including the methods of encouragement to adhere to the prescribed daily pills. The randomization scheme in each study can be viewed as a different version of an IV.
3. Implementation trials. Implementation science studies methods to promote the systematic uptake of evidence based interventions (Wolfenden et al., 2021). An implementation trial that compares different methods to encourage treatment uptake often induces nested IV structures.

A nested IV assumption, when specialized to (1) a pooled analysis of a multicentre clinical trial, (2) an integrated analysis of multiple studies, or (3) an implementation trial comparing different encouragement strategies, would state that a participant who was a complier when enrolled in a clinical site or study with a lower compliance rate would remain a complier had the person enrolled in a clinical site or study with a higher compliance rate.

# 1.3 Implications of a nested IV assumption 

While a conventional IV analysis defines latent subpopulations - compliers, always-takers, nevertakers, and defiers - based on potential treatment received under two realizations of one binary IV (Angrist et al., 1996), the nested IV assumption and its associated framework would define subpopulations based on potential treatment received under $2 \times 2=4$ realizations of two binary IVs and impose structures on these latent subpopulations in a way analogous to the monotonicity assumption in the original paper by Angrist et al. (1996). Under the nested IV framework, the average treatment effects of two latent subpopulations, referred to as "always-compliers" and "switchers," respectively, can be non-parametrically identified under suitable conditions. "Always-compliers" are participants who would comply with the treatment regardless of the specific IV being used; for instance, these are participants who would be compliers regardless of the consent process employed or the clinical site at which they were enrolled. On the other hand, a non-overlapping latent subpopulation called "switchers" are participants who would be a non-complier (i.e., an always-taker or a never-taker under Angrist et al.'s (1996) monotonicity assumption) under the weaker IV but become a complier under a strengthened IV; in the PLCO trial, these are participants who would not comply under a dual consent process but comply under a single consent process. In addition

to identifying and estimating the causal effect among "always-compliers" and "switchers," a comparison of the causal effects on these two disjoint subpopulations, possibly conditional on a set of baseline covariates, helps illuminate the generalizability of IV-based estimates and formally test the no-interaction/principal-ignorability-type assumptions. The proposed tests are flexible nonparametric generalizations of classical over-identification tests that incorporate machine learning tools for the estimation of nuisance parameters. Such progress towards establishing the generalizability of IV estimates, to the best of our knowledge, is a novel and useful contribution to the literature.

The rest of the article is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe the nested IV design, define the switcher average treatment effect (SWATE) and present main identification results. In Section 4, we propose estimators for SWATE. In Section 5, we propose formal hypothesis testing procedures that examine treatment effect homogeneity among latent subpopulations under the proposed nested IV framework. Numerical experiments are reported in Section 6. We examine the PLCO study using our proposed method and framework in Section 7 and conclude with a discussion in Section 8.

# 2 Nested IV design
### 2.1 Two versions of treatment assignment

Consider a clinical trial centre in the PLCO study, say the Henry Ford Health System, that switched from a dual to a single consent process. The clinical trial comprised two stages. Let $G=a$ denote the dual consent stage, and we use $Z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ to denote a participant being randomized to the control group $\left(Z=0_{a}\right)$ or the intervention group $\left(Z=1_{a}\right)$ in the dual consent stage. In parallel, in the single consent stage, denoted by $G=b$, we use $Z \in\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$ to denote a participant being randomized to the control $\left(Z=0_{b}\right)$ group or the intervention $\left(Z=1_{b}\right)$ group. Importantly, in either stage, participants randomized to the intervention arm may choose not to take the assigned cancer screening procedure, while participants randomized to the control arm may choose to conduct a cancer screening even if this is not part of their usual medical care. In other words, the randomized treatment assignment is only an encouragement, or a nudge, for participants to receive cancer screening, and participants retain the full right not to adhere to the treatment assignment.

Treatment assignment, or "encouragement to receive the treatment," may carry different implications in two trial stages $(G=a$ or $G=b)$ and hence resulted in different compliance rates; therefore, we use different notations, $1_{a}$ and $1_{b}$ (or $0_{a}$ and $0_{b}$ ), to denote being assigned to the intervention (or control) arm and encouraged to receive cancer screening (or usual care). Our notation acknowledges that there may exist two versions of encouragement and that the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (Rubin, 1974, 1980), or SUTVA, may be violated if one single notation ( 0 or 1 ) is used instead.

To further fix ideas, consider a second example in the context of HIV prevention implementation trials (Lambdin et al., 2015). To best leverage the multiple effective HIV prevention modalities in the real world settings, scientists are studying the best implementation strategies to encourage people at elevated HIV risk to use the appropriate HIV prevention tools, like daily oral prophylaxis. To this end, trials with different mechanisms to improve drug uptake (e.g., different drug delivery methods) are deployed. In this context, one could use $G=a$ or $G=b$ to denote two separate implementation trials, $Z=1_{a}$ or $Z=0_{a}$ to denote randomization to a first drug delivery method or a control method, and $Z=1_{b}$ or $Z=0_{b}$ to denote randomization to a second drug delivery method or a possibly different control method.

# 2.2 Potential outcomes and identification assumptions 

We define potential outcomes and formulate causal estimands under Neyman and Rubin's potential outcomes framework (Neyman, 1923; Rubin, 1974). Suppose we observe $n$ independent and identically distributed samples, $\mathcal{D}=\left\{O_{i}=\left(Z_{i}, \boldsymbol{X}_{i}, D_{i}, Y_{i}\right), i=1, \ldots, n\right\}$, from a target population $P_{0} \in \mathcal{P}$, where $\mathcal{P}$ denotes a non-parametric model for the observed data distribution. Throughout the article, we use $\mathbb{E}_{P}[\cdot]$ to denote taking expectation over some distribution $P \in \mathcal{P}$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[\cdot]$ taking expectation over the target population. For participant $i, \boldsymbol{X}_{i}$ denotes a set of baseline covariates, $Z_{i}$ a categorical instrumental variable taking value in $\left\{0_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{a}, 1_{b}\right\}, D_{i} \in\{0,1\}$ a binary variable indicating the treatment a participant actually received, and $Y_{i}$ a real-valued outcome of interest. Let $G_{i}$ denote a stratification variable, that is, define $G_{i}=a$ if $Z_{i} \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$, and $G_{i}=b$ if $Z_{i} \in\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$. For the Henry Ford Health System in the PLCO study, $G_{i}$ denotes the trial stage and, consequently, the type of consent process used (e.g., dual or single consent). In the context of an across-center or across-trial integrated analysis, $G_{i}$ would represent the clinical center or the

specific trial in which a participant was enrolled.
We will refer to the tuple $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right)\left(\right.$ or $\left.\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)\right)$ as an IV dose pair (Sun and Wüthrich, 2022). We use $Y(D=d, Z=z)$ to denote the potential outcome of $Y$ when a participant is assigned $D=d$ and $Z=z$ and $D(Z=z)$ to denote potential outcome of $D$ when a participant is assigned $Z=z$. We write $Y(Z=z)$ as a shorthand of $Y(D(Z=z), Z=z)$. Following Angrist et al. (1996), we say a participant is a complier under the IV dose pair $\left\{0_{g}, 1_{g}\right\}$ if $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{g}\right), D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)\right\}=(0,1)$, an always-taker if $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{g}\right), D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)\right\}=(1,1)$, a never-taker if $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{g}\right), D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)\right\}=(0,0)$, or a defier if $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{g}\right), D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)\right\}=(1,0), g \in\{a, b\}$. We first describe identification assumptions.

# Assumption 1. (Standard IV assumptions). 

(i). (Consistency). $D=D(Z=z)$ if $Z=z, Y=Y(D=d, Z=z)$ if $D=d$ and $Z=z$, for $d \in\{0,1\}$ and $z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$.
(ii). (Exclusion restriction). $Y(D=d, Z=z)=Y\left(D=d, Z=z^{\prime}\right)$, for $d \in\{0,1\}$ and $z, z^{\prime} \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$.
(iii). (IV independence). $Z \Perp \{\{D(Z=z), Y(D=d)\} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{X}, G=g$, for all $d, z$ and $g$.
(iv). (IV relevance). $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=1_{g}, \boldsymbol{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=0_{g}, \boldsymbol{X}\right] \neq 0$ and $P_{0}(Z=z \mid \boldsymbol{X})>0$ for $g \in\{a, b\}, z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$.

All four parts of Assumption 1 are standard IV identification assumptions and sometimes referred to as core IV assumptions (Angrist et al., 1996; Baiocchi et al., 2014). In a clinical trial like the PLCO study, the treatment assignment is most likely affecting clinical outcomes only via its effect on the treatment received, so exclusion restriction (Assumption 1(ii)) is often satisfied. We will use notation $Y(D=d)$ as a shorthand of $Y(D=d, Z=z)$ since the latter does not depend on $z$ by exclusion restriction. Moreover, IV independence (Assumption 1(iii)) is automatically satisfied by design in a randomized trial, and IV relevance (Assumption 1(iv)) is verifiable and holds in most clinical trials.

In the nested IV framework, the IV dose pair that a participant receives depends on the stratification variable $G$ : a participant will be randomly assigned to $0_{a}$ or $1_{a}$ if $G=a$, or $0_{b}$ or $1_{b}$ if $G=b$. In addition to the core IV assumptions, we consider the following set of nested IV assumptions:

# Assumption 2. (Nested IV assumptions). 

(i). (Mean exchangeability over $G$ ). $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y\left(Z=1_{g}\right)-Y\left(Z=0_{g}\right) \mid G=g, \boldsymbol{X}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(Z=$ $\left.1_{g}\right)-Y\left(Z=0_{g}\right) \mid \boldsymbol{X}]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)-D\left(Z=0_{g}\right) \mid G=g, \boldsymbol{X}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)-D(Z=\right.$ $\left.0_{g}\right) \mid \boldsymbol{X}], g \in\{a, b\}$.
(ii). (Partial monotonicity). $D\left(Z=1_{g}\right) \geq D\left(Z=0_{g}\right), g \in\{a, b\}$.
(iii). (Non-equal compliance).

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right] \\
\neq \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

(iv). (Nested IV). $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{a}\right), D\left(Z=1_{a}\right)\right\}=(0,1)$ implies $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{b}\right), D\left(Z=1_{b}\right)\right\}=(0,1)$.

Assumption 2(i) states that, conditional on the observed covariates $\boldsymbol{X}$, the average effect of IV $Z$ (either version) on $D$ and that on $Y$ can be identified based on the corresponding stratum $G=a$ or $b$. This assumption is satisfied if the stratification variable $G$ is exogenous. For instance, in the PLCO study, the sudden shift from dual to single consent could be thought of as a happenstance for participants who enrolled right before and after this policy shift, analogous to the so-called "regression discontinuity design" (Thistlethwaite and Campbell, 1960). This assumption is also satisfied, for example, if participating in the trial does not itself modify the effect of the IV on $D$ (the treatment) or $Y$ (the outcome), which is a standard assumption in the literature on generalizability (Dahabreh et al., 2019). Assumption 2(ii) states that there is no defier with respect to either version of the IV. Importantly, we do not impose any ordering among $\left\{0_{a}, 0_{b}\right\},\left\{0_{a}, 1_{b}\right\},\left\{1_{a}, 0_{b}\right\}$, or $\left\{1_{a}, 1_{b}\right\}$; hence, this partial monotonicity assumption is weaker than the usual monotonicity assumption for an ordinal IV (Imbens and Angrist, 1994). Assumption 2(iii) states that the compliance rates corresponding to $G=a$ and $G=b$ are different; this is likely to hold when the IV is of different versions in two strata. Finally, Assumption 2(iv) states that if a participant is a complier under the IV pair $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$, then the participant is also a complier under the IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$. This assumption is key to our identification results and most likely to be satisfied when the binary IV $Z \in\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$ is stronger than the binary IV $Z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$. Empirically, the compliance rates can be calculated for

both IV pairs, either marginally or conditional on a set of covariates as in Marcus et al. (2014), so the reasonableness of Assumption 2(iv) can be assessed prior to invoking the nested IV framework.

# 2.3 Principal strata; causal estimands; identification results 

A total of $2^{4}=16$ possible subgroups can be defined based on the joint potential outcomes

$$
\left\{D\left(Z=0_{a}\right), D\left(Z=1_{a}\right), D\left(Z=0_{b}\right), D\left(Z=1_{b}\right)\right\}
$$

see Table 1. Assumptions 2(ii) (partial monotonicity) and 2(iv) (nested IV) together eliminate 9 out of 16 principal strata, and the population then consists of the following 6 latent subgroups:

1. Always-Aways-Takers (AAT): Always-takers under both IV pairs $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ and $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$;
2. SWitchers (SW): Always-takers or never-takers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ but compliers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$;
3. Always-Taker-Never-Taker (AT-NT): Always-takers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ but nevertakers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$;
4. Always-COmplier (ACO): Compliers under both IV pairs $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ and $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$;
5. Never-Taker-AIways-Taker (NT-AT): Never-takers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ but alwaystakers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$;
6. Always-Never-Taker (ANT): Never-takers under both IV pairs $\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ and $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$.

Remark 1 (One-sided non-compliance). In clinical trials assessing an investigational product, participants assigned placebo often do not have access to the treatment. This is referred to as "onesided non-compliance." In this stylistic case, we necessarily have $D\left(Z=0_{a}\right)=D\left(Z=0_{b}\right)=0$, and the latent groups $N T-A T, A T-N T$ and $A A T$ in Table 1 no longer exist. Moreover, the switcher subgroup now only comprises participants who are never-takers under $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right)$ but become compliers under $\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)$.

Let $S$ denote principal stratum. Define the following conditional switcher average treatment effect:

$$
\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}, \boldsymbol{X}]
$$

and the conditional always-complier average treatment effect:

$$
\operatorname{ACOATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{ACO}, \boldsymbol{X}]
$$

Importantly, both $\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ and $\operatorname{ACOATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ are the average "per-protocol" effect of $D$ on $Y$, although on different subpopulations, within strata defined by observed covariates $\boldsymbol{X}$. Averaging $\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ and $\operatorname{ACOATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ then yields the SWitcher Average Treatment Effect (SWATE):

$$
\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}:=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}]
$$

and the Always-COmplier Average Treatment Effect (ACOATE):

$$
\operatorname{ACOATE}_{P_{0}}:=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{ACO}]
$$

Theorem 1 is our main identification result and shows that the ACOATE and SWATE can be non-

parametrically identified from observed data under identification assumptions discussed in Section 2.2.

Theorem 1. Under Assumptions 1(i)-(iv) and 2(i)-(iv), $S W A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x}), A C O A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x}), S W A T E_{P_{0}}$ and $A C O A T E_{P_{0}}$ can be non-parametrically identified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A C O A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=\theta_{A C O, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\frac{\delta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})} ; \quad S W A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=\theta_{S W, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\frac{\delta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\delta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})} ; \\
& A C O A T E_{P_{0}}=\Psi_{A C O, P_{0}}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\delta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]} ; \quad S W A T E_{P_{0}}=\Psi_{S W, P_{0}}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\delta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\delta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}
\end{aligned}
$$

where, for $P \in \mathcal{P}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \delta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{x}):=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right] \\
& \delta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{x}):=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right] \\
& \eta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{x}):=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[D \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[D \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right] \\
& \eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{x}):=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[D \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[D \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Unlike ACOATE or SWATE, the causal effect in other latent subgroups, including AAT, AT-NT, NT-AT, and ANT, cannot be non-parametrically identified.

# 2.4 Conventional Wald estimator when SUTVA is violated 

A conventional IV analysis that ignores different versions of an IV would define a binary IV $Z^{*}$ as follows: $Z^{*}=1$ if $Z=1_{a}$ or $Z=1_{b}$, and $Z^{*}=0$ if $Z=0_{a}$ or $Z=0_{b}$. The analysis would then identify the conditional complier average treatment effect using the following Wald estimator (Frölich, 2007):

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{CW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1, \boldsymbol{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0, \boldsymbol{X}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1, \boldsymbol{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0, \boldsymbol{X}\right]}
$$

As we have discussed extensively in Section 2.1, the potential outcomes $Y\left(Z^{*}=z^{*}\right)$ and $D\left(Z^{*}=z^{*}\right)$, $z^{*} \in\{0,1\}$, are not well-defined as SUTVA is violated. Nevertheless, the statistical functional in (1) is well-defined, and it is of interest to understand its meaning. Our next result states that, under an additional testable assumption $G \Perp Z^{*} \mid \boldsymbol{X}$, this "conventional Wald estimand" can be

interpreted as a weighted average of conditional ACOATE and conditional SWATE:

Proposition 1. Under Assumption 1, Assumption 2, and an additional assumption $G \Perp Z^{*} \mid \boldsymbol{X}$, we have

$$
\theta_{C W, P_{0}}(X)=\omega_{1} \cdot S W A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})+\omega_{2} \cdot A C O A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \omega_{1}=\frac{P_{0}(S=S W \mid \boldsymbol{X}) P_{0}(G=b \mid \boldsymbol{X})}{P_{0}(S=S W \mid \boldsymbol{X}) P_{0}(G=b \mid \boldsymbol{X})+P_{0}(S=A C O \mid \boldsymbol{X})}, \text { and } \\
& \omega_{2}=\frac{P_{0}(S=A C O \mid \boldsymbol{X})}{P_{0}(S=S W \mid \boldsymbol{X}) P_{0}(G=b \mid \boldsymbol{X})+P_{0}(S=A C O \mid \boldsymbol{X})}
\end{aligned}
$$

The additional assumption $G \Perp Z^{*} \mid \boldsymbol{X}$ is equivalent to stating that the treatment assignment probability does not depend on the stratification variable (e.g., study stage or clinical center). That is, $P_{0}\left(Z=1_{a} \mid G=a, \boldsymbol{X}\right)=P_{0}\left(Z=1_{b} \mid G=b, \boldsymbol{X}\right)$ and $P_{0}\left(Z=0_{a} \mid G=a, \boldsymbol{X}\right)=P_{0}\left(Z=0_{b} \mid G=\right.$ $b, \boldsymbol{X})$. This assumption is testable and holds in the PLCO trial as $Z$ is randomized in each study stage. It should be noted that the marginalized Wald estimand, defined as

$$
\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1, \boldsymbol{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0, \boldsymbol{X}\right]\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1, \boldsymbol{X}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0, \boldsymbol{X}\right]\right]}
$$

does not equal a weighted average of SWATE and ACOATE in general.

# 2.5 Practical relevance of ACOATE and SWATE 

Causal estimands ACOATE and SWATE are examples of the so-called principal treatment effects (Frangakis and Rubin, 2002). As discussed in Section 1.1, the practical relevance of any principal stratum effects is always under close scrutiny and often with good reasons (Pearl, 2011; Dawid and Didelez, 2012). Responding to Pearl's (2011) critiques, in our opinion, SWATE and ACOATE are both a useful "tool" in a holistic IV analysis and potentially interesting causal parameters in themselves. First, it is a "tool" towards establishing the generalizability of a causal effect. For instance, researchers can immediately get a crude assessment of the generalizability of the treatment effect by comparing ACOATE to SWATE conditional on $\boldsymbol{X}$. Such a testing strategy could be more

powerful than directly comparing the treatment effects among compliers under two versions of the IV. We will develop a formal testing procedure for the principal ignorability assumption in Section 5. Moreover, the ACOATE and SWATE help unravel additional effect heterogeneity and could be more informative than the standard CATE. Although a study participant cannot be classified into one of the latent subgroups, the distribution of observed covariates among always-compliers and switchers can be characterized. Proposition 2 gives an identification formula for a function of an observed covariate among always-compliers and switchers.

Proposition 2. Let $g(\cdot)$ denote a generic function. The mean of $g(\boldsymbol{X})$ among switchers and always-compliers can be identified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[g(\boldsymbol{X}) \mid S=S W]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[g(\boldsymbol{X}) \frac{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}\right] \\
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[g(\boldsymbol{X}) \mid S=A C O]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[g(\boldsymbol{X}) \frac{\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Based on Proposition 2, the mean and variance of each observed covariate, and more generally certain combinations of observed covariates (e.g., a projected risk score), in the always-complier and switcher subgroups can be characterized and compared to those in the entire study population. For instance, for a binary covariate $X$, a "prevalence ratio" (Brookhart and Schneeweiss, 2007) may be calculated as $P_{0}(X=1 \mid S=\mathrm{ACO}) / P_{0}(X=1)$ and $P_{0}(X=1 \mid S=\mathrm{SW}) / P_{0}(X=1)$.

# 3 Extensions
### 3.1 Vector IV representation and connection to vector IV literature

So far, we have formulated $Z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$ as a categorical IV. An alternative approach is to define a vector-valued IV, denoted as $\left(Z^{*}, G\right)$, where $Z^{*} \in\{0,1\}$ indicates whether an individual is assigned to the treatment group or the control group, and $G$ is the stratification variable, which takes values in $\{a, b\}$. For $G=g \in\{a, b\}$, one may alternatively write $D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)$ as $D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=g\right)$ and $D\left(Z=0_{g}\right)$ as $D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=g\right)$. Under this vector IV representation, we may compare our partial monotonicity assumption (denoted as PM) to (1) the partial monotonicity assumption in

Mogstad et al. (2021) (denoted as PM2); (2) the limited monotonicity assumption in Hoff et al. (2024) (denoted as LiM); and (3) the vector monotonicity assumption in Goff (2024) (denoted as VM), when both $Z^{*}$ and $G$ are binary. In the Supplemental Material S1.1, we review these identification assumptions and discuss their relationship in detail. We show that PM2 and VM are equivalent in our setting, and PM, PM2 (VM) and LiM imply different principal strata. Moreover, the collection of 7 principal strata implied by the PM plus the nested IV assumption is neither a superset nor a subset of the principal strata implied by PM2 (VM) or LiM, highlighting the novelty of the identification assumptions developed in this article. In the Supplemental Material S1.2, we also discussed the difference between the SWATE and principal strata effects proposed in Goff (2024).

# 3.2 Sensitivity of the estimand to violation of the nested IV assumption 

We consider violations of the nested IV assumption. When the nested IV assumption fails, two additional principal strata, those with $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{a}\right)=0, D\left(Z=1_{a}\right)=1, D\left(Z=0_{b}\right)=0, D(Z=\right.$ $\left.1_{b}\right)=0\}$ or $\left\{D\left(Z=0_{a}\right)=0, D\left(Z=1_{a}\right)=1, D\left(Z=0_{b}\right)=1, D\left(Z=1_{b}\right)=1\right\}$, will come into existence. We refer to the union of these two principal strata as DeFiers to the Nested IV assumption (DFN).

Proposition 3. Under Assumption 1 (i)-(iv) and 2(i)-(iii), but without the nested IV assumption, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\theta_{S W, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x}) \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=S W, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]+ \\
\left\{1-\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})\right\} \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=D F N, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

where

$$
\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac{P_{0}(S=S W \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x})}{P_{0}(S=S W \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x})+P_{0}(S=D F N \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x})}
$$

Proposition 3 states that without the nested IV assumption, the statistical functional $\theta_{S W, P_{0}}$ equals a weighted average of the conditional average treatment effect of switchers (SW) and DFN. Under

the nested IV assumption, $P_{0}(S=\mathrm{DFN} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x})=0, \lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=1$, and therefore the statistical functional $\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ identifies $\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$. It should be noted that $\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x}) \in[0,1]$; therefore, $\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ lies in the convex hull of $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=$ 1) $-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{DFN}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]$. Proposition 3 also implies that if we assume effect homogeneity among SW and DFN, that is, $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=$ 1) $-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{DFN}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]$, then $\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ can still be identified by $\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$.

Rearranging (7) yields:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}] \\
=-\left\{1-\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})\right\}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{SW}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]-\right. \\
\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{DFN}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]\}
\end{gathered}
$$

which gives the bias formula when the nested IV assumption is violated. In practice, expression (3) can be used as a basis for a sensitivity analysis by specifying $\lambda_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=$ 0) $\mid S=\mathrm{DFN}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]$ as sensitivity functions (see, e.g., Brumback et al. (2004)).

# 3.3 Multiple IV pairs; ordinal IV; strengthening an IV 

The nested IV framework can be extended to multiple IV pairs. Let $Z \in \mathcal{Z}$ denote an IV, where $\mathcal{Z}$ is the support of $Z$. Throughout this subsection, we assume consistency, exclusion restriction and IV independence assumptions hold for any $z \in \mathcal{Z}$, so $Z$ is a valid IV. Let $\mathcal{G}$ denote an index set, and $0_{g}$ and $1_{g}$ denote two distinct elements of $\mathcal{Z}$, where $g \in \mathcal{G}$ is the index. The ordered pair $\left(0_{g}, 1_{g}\right)$ is referred to as an IV pair, denoted as $\mathcal{Z}_{g}$, if $D\left(1_{g}\right) \geq D\left(0_{g}\right)$. Definition 1 formally defines a nested IV relation.

Definition 1. (Nested IV relation). Let $g, g^{\prime} \in \mathcal{G}$. IV pair $\mathcal{Z}_{g}$ is said to be nested within IV pair $\mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$, denoted as $\mathcal{Z}_{g} \preceq \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$, if $\left\{\left(D\left(0_{g}\right), D\left(1_{g}\right)\right)=(0,1)\right\} \subset\left\{\left(D\left(0_{g^{\prime}}\right), D\left(1_{g^{\prime}}\right)\right)=(0,1)\right\}$. We also define $\mathcal{Z}_{g} \succeq \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ if $\mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}} \preceq \mathcal{Z}_{g}$, and $\mathcal{Z}_{g} \sim \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ if both $\mathcal{Z}_{g} \succeq \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ and $\mathcal{Z}_{g} \preceq \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ hold.

The nested IV relation is a binary relation defined on the set of all IV pairs $\mathcal{F}:=\left\{\mathcal{Z}_{g}, g \in\right.$ $\mathcal{G}\}$. Proposition 4 states the properties of the nested IV relation, which follows directly from the Definition 1.

Proposition 4. The nested IV relation $\preceq$, as defined in Definition 1, is reflexive, transitive, but not necessarily complete. The relation " $\sim$ " defines an equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$.

Suppose IV pair $\mathcal{Z}_{g}$ is nested in IV pair $\mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$, the switcher associated with IV pairs $\mathcal{Z}_{g}, \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ is defined as

$$
\left\{D\left(1_{g^{\prime}}\right)=1, D\left(0_{g^{\prime}}\right)=0\right\} \backslash\left\{D\left(1_{g}\right)=1, D\left(0_{g}\right)=0\right\}
$$

We can similarly define the SWATE associated with IV pairs $\mathcal{Z}_{g}, \mathcal{Z}_{g^{\prime}}$ as in section 2.2. Since the SWATE is always defined with respect to two IV pairs, in the following sections we will focus on two IV pairs.

Formalizing the nested IV assumption as a binary relation is useful conceptually when the stratification variable $G$ takes on multiple values. Below, we give three examples.

Example 1 (Multicentre clinical trials). When the objective is to pool data across clinical sites with varying degrees of compliance to estimate the switcher treatment effect, then $G$ represents different clinical sites. For instance, in the PLCO study, when the Henry Ford Health System adopted a dual consent process, two other sites, University of Colorado (UC) and University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), both adopted a single consent process and had a high compliance rate. As we will demonstrate in the case study (Section 7), one may do an integrated data analysis by defining the stratification variable $G \in\{a, b, c\}$, where $G=a$ corresponds to Henry Ford, $G=b$ $U C$, and $G=c U A B$. In this analysis, $\mathcal{Z}=\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}, 0_{c}, 1_{c}\right\}$, and it is reasonable to assume the IV pair $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right)$ is nested within both $\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)$, denoted $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right) \preceq\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)$, and $\left(0_{c}, 1_{c}\right)$, denoted $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right) \preceq\left(0_{c}, 1_{c}\right)$, without imposing any relation between $\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)$ and $\left(0_{c}, 1_{c}\right)$ because the nested IV assumption may not hold for UC and UAB participants. When viewed as a partial order, both $\left(0_{b}, 1_{b}\right)$ and $\left(0_{c}, 1_{c}\right)$ are maximal elements.

Example 2 (Ordinal IV). An ordinal IV can be understood as a collection of IV pairs, equipped with a nested IV relation. For instance, let $Z \in\{0,1,2\}$ be an ordinal IV with three levels. Suppose $D(Z)$ is binary, $D(z) \geq D\left(z^{\prime}\right)$ if $z \geq z^{\prime}$, and the population consists of a mixture of those with $(D(0), D(1), D(2))=(0,0,0),(0,0,1),(0,1,1)$, and $(1,1,1)$. This three-level ordinal IV can be decomposed into the following three IV pairs: $(0,1),(1,2)$, and $(0,2)$. Among the three IV pairs, we

have the following nested IV relations: $(0,1) \preceq(0,2),(1,2) \preceq(0,2)$; however, neither $(0,1) \succeq(1,2)$ nor $(0,1) \preceq(1,2)$ holds.

Example 3 (Strengthening an IV). A nested IV relation helps understand how an ordinal or continuous IV could be strengthened in a matched cohort study (Baiocchi et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2024). Let $Z \in[0,1]$ denote a continuous IV. Suppose the treatment uptake $D(z)$ is determined by some latent continuous variable $D^{*}(z)$ by $D(z)=\mathbb{1}\left\{D^{*}(z) \geq \frac{3}{4}\right\}$. Suppose the population consists of (1) those with $D^{*}(z)=z$; and (2) those with $D^{*}(z)=\frac{1}{2} z+\frac{1}{2}$. The set of IV pairs can then be defined as $\{(a, b): 0 \leq a \leq b \leq 1\}$. One may easily verify, for instance, that $\left(0, \frac{1}{3}\right)$ is nested in $\left(0, \frac{2}{3}\right)$, and $\left(\frac{2}{3}, 1\right)$ is nested in $\left(\frac{1}{3}, 1\right)$. Consider four participants with the same observed covariates to be matched, with $Z \in\{0,1 / 3,2 / 3,1\}$. By pairing the participant with $Z=0$ with $Z=2 / 3$, and $Z=1 / 3$ with $Z=1$, one may construct a matched cohort with higher compliance rate, compared to pairing $Z=0$ with $Z=1 / 3$ and $Z=2 / 3$ with $Z=1$, as advocated in Baiocchi et al. (2010).

# 4 Estimation and inference 

Estimation of the always-complier average treatment effect follows immediately by applying the estimation and inferential methods in the standard IV literature to the binary IV pair $\left(0_{a}, 1_{a}\right)$; see, e.g., Frölich (2007) and Kennedy (2022). In this section, we will focus on estimation and inference of the switcher average treatment effect.

### 4.1 Wald-type estimator

When the IV assignment is randomized between and within each stratum $(G=a$ or $b)$, as in a randomized clinical trial, a classical Wald estimator for ACOATE is $\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{ACO}}^{\mathrm{Wald}}=\frac{\widehat{\delta}_{a}}{\widehat{\eta}_{a}}$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{\delta}_{a}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=1_{a}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=1_{a}} Y_{i}-\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=0_{a}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=0_{a}} Y_{i} \\
& \widehat{\eta}_{a}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=1_{a}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=1_{a}} D_{i}-\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=0_{a}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=0_{a}} D_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

An analogous Wald-type estimator for SWATE can be formulated as follows:

$$
\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{SW}}^{\mathrm{Wald}}=\frac{\widehat{\delta}_{b}-\widehat{\delta}_{a}}{\widehat{\eta}_{b}-\widehat{\eta}_{a}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{\delta}_{b}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=1_{b}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=1_{b}} Y_{i}-\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=0_{b}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=0_{b}} Y_{i} \\
& \widehat{\eta}_{b}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=1_{b}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=1_{b}} D_{i}-\frac{1}{\sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\left\{Z_{i}=0_{b}\right\}} \sum_{Z_{i}=0_{b}} D_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

Theorem 2 summarizes the property of $\widehat{\psi}_{\mathrm{SW}}^{\mathrm{Wald}}$.

Theorem 2. Under regularity conditions specified in Supplemental Material S2.5, we have

$$
\sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\psi}_{S W}^{W a l d d}-\Psi_{S W, P_{0}}\right) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sigma_{W a l d}^{2}\right)
$$

where $\sigma_{W a l d}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\varphi_{W a l d, S W}^{2}\right]$, and $\varphi_{\text {Wald,SW }}$ is the influence function of $\widehat{\psi}_{S W}^{\text {Wald }}$, whose form can be found in Supplemental Material S2.5.

An estimator $\widehat{\sigma}_{\text {Wald }}^{2}$ of $\sigma_{\text {Wald }}^{2}$ can be obtained using non-parametric bootstrap or via the delta method.

# 4.2 Non-parametric efficiency bound 

We now derive the non-parametric efficiency bound for the target identified parameter $\Psi_{S W, P_{0}}$ under identification assumptions discussed in Section 2.2. For a pathwise differentiable parameter, its nonparametric efficiency bound equals the variance of the canonical gradient at $P_{0}$ in a non-parametric model. Theorem 3 derives the canonical gradient and hence the non-parametric efficiency bound for the identification functional $\Psi_{S W, P}$.

Theorem 3. The canonical gradient of

$$
\Psi_{S W, P}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\delta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{X})-\delta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}
$$

at $P_{0}$ is $D_{P_{0}}$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{P} & =(z, x, d, y) \mapsto \frac{1}{\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}\left\{\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{P\left(Z=1_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right]\right. \\
& -\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}}{P\left(Z=0_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right] \\
& -\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{a}\right\}}{P\left(Z=1_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right]+\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{a}\right\}}{P\left(Z=0_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[Y \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right] \\
& \left.+\delta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{x})-\delta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{x})\right\}-\frac{\Psi_{S W, P}}{\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]}\left\{\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{P\left(Z=1_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left(D \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right]\right. \\
& -\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}}{P\left(Z=0_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left(D \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right]-\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{Z=1_{a}\right\}}{P\left(Z=1_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left(D \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right] \\
& \left.+\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{Z=0_{a}\right\}}{P\left(Z=0_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left(D \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right]+\eta_{b, P}(\boldsymbol{x})-\eta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{x})\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the non-parametric efficiency bound is $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D_{P_{0}}^{2}(Z, X, D, Y)\right]$.

# 4.3 Non-parametric efficient estimators 

The efficient influence function in Theorem 3 motivates an asymptotically efficient, one-step estimator and an estimating equation-based estimator. A one-step estimator is based on first order bias correction of a plug-in estimator (Pfanzagl, 1990); an estimating equation-based estimator is based on solving an efficient influence function-based estimating equation (van der Laan and Robins, 2003; Chernozhukov et al., 2018a). Here we will focus on the estimating equation-based estimator and leave the one-step estimator to Supplemental Material S2.7.

Define

$$
\begin{gathered}
\pi_{P}=\left(\pi_{0_{a}, P}, \pi_{0_{b}, P}, \pi_{0_{b}, P}, \pi_{1_{b}, P}\right), \text { where } \pi_{z, P}=P(Z=z \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}) \\
\mu_{Y, P}=\left(\mu_{Y, 0_{a}, P}, \mu_{Y, 1_{b}, P}, \mu_{Y, 0_{b}, P}, \mu_{Y, 1_{b}, P}\right), \text { where } \mu_{Y, z, P}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[Y \mid Z=z, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}] \\
\mu_{D, P}=\left(\mu_{D, 0_{a}, P}, \mu_{D, 1_{b}, P}, \mu_{D, 0_{b}, P}, \mu_{D, 1_{b}, P}\right), \text { where } \mu_{D, z, P}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[D \mid Z=z, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]
\end{gathered}
$$

for $z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}, 0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$. The canonical gradient defines an estimating function of $\Psi_{P_{0}}$, denoted as

$D^{\prime}\left(o ; \Psi_{P}, \pi_{P}, \mu_{Y, P}, \mu_{D, P}\right)$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D^{\prime}\left(o ; \Psi_{P}, \pi_{P}, \mu_{Y, P}, \mu_{D, P}\right) \\
= & \left\{\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{\pi_{1_{b}, P}(x)}\left[y-\mu_{Y, 1_{b}, P}(x)\right]-\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}}{\pi_{0_{b}, P}(x)}\left[y-\mu_{Y, 0_{b}, P}(x)\right]-\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{a}\right\}}{\pi_{1_{a}, P}(x)}\left[y-\mu_{Y, 1_{a}, P}(x)\right]\right. \\
+ & \left.\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{a}\right\}}{\pi_{0_{a}, P}(x)}\left[y-\mu_{Y, 0_{a}, P}(x)\right]+\delta_{b_{P}}(\boldsymbol{x})-\delta_{a, P}(\boldsymbol{x})\right\}-\Psi_{S W, P}\left\{\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{\pi_{1_{b}, P}(x)}\left[d-\mu_{D, 1_{b}, P}(x)\right]\right. \\

Consider a $K$-fold random partition $\left\{I_{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{K}$ of indices $[N]=\{1, \ldots, K\}$, and define $I_{k}^{c}:=$ $\{1, \ldots, n\}-I_{k}$. # 5 Testable implications of homogeneity-type assumptions in the nested IV design
### 5.1 Generalizing principal stratum effects

Let $\operatorname{ATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]$ denote the conditional average treatment effect among those with covariates $\boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\operatorname{ATE}_{P_{0}}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\operatorname{ATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]$. Proposition 5 states two sufficient conditions that facilitates identifying $\operatorname{ATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ (and hence $\operatorname{ATE}_{P_{0}}$ ) from principal stratum effect $\mathrm{ACOATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ or $\operatorname{SWATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$.

Proposition 5. Suppose one of the following assumptions holds:
H(i). (Principal ignorability) $\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=d) \mid S=s, \boldsymbol{X}]=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=d) \mid \boldsymbol{X}]$ for $d \in\{0,1\}$.
H(ii). (No unmeasured common effect modifier)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Cov}_{P_{0}}\left[\left(D\left(Z=1_{a}\right)-D\left(Z=0_{a}\right)\right)(Y(D=1)-Y(D=0)) \mid \boldsymbol{X}\right]=0 \\
& \operatorname{Cov}_{P_{0}}\left[\left(D\left(Z=1_{b}\right)-D\left(Z=0_{b}\right)\right)(Y(D=1)-Y(D=0)) \mid \boldsymbol{X}\right]=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have $A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=A C O A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})=S W A T E_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$.

Remark 3 (Single IV setting). Both Assumption H(i) and Assumption H(ii) in Proposition 5 have their counterparts in the usual setting with one IV; see, e.g., Jo and Stuart (2009) and Wang and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2018). With one IV, either assumption implies that the conditional complier average treatment effect with respect to the IV equals the conditional average treatment effect.

Define $\operatorname{COATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S \in\{\mathrm{SW}, \mathrm{ACO}\}, \boldsymbol{X}]$, which is the conditional average treatment effect among compliers under IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$. Then under Assumptions 1 and 2, we have $\operatorname{COATE}_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=\theta_{\mathrm{CO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}):=\frac{\delta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}$. Observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{\mathrm{CO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X}) & :=\frac{\delta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})} \\
& =\left\{\frac{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}\right\} \times \theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})+\left\{\frac{\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})}\right\} \times \theta_{\mathrm{ACO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})
\end{aligned}
$$

Under the nested IV setting, Proposition 5 implies that Assumption $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{i})$ or $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{ii})$ has the following testable implications: $\theta_{P_{0}}^{(1)} \equiv \theta_{\mathrm{ACO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=0$ a.s. $P_{0}, \theta_{P_{0}}^{(2)} \equiv \theta_{\mathrm{ACO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\theta_{\mathrm{CO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=$ 0 a.s. $P_{0}$, and $\theta_{P_{0}}^{(3)} \equiv \theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\theta_{\mathrm{CO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$. In words, under either assumption, we would expect that, within strata of $\boldsymbol{X}$, the average treatment effect among always-compliers equals that among the switchers and that among the compliers under the IV pair $\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$.

Next, we propose formal statistical procedures testing the null hypothesis:

$$
H_{0}^{(j)}: \theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}=0 \text { a.s. } P_{0} \text { vs } H_{1}^{(j)}: \theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)} \neq 0, \quad j=1,2,3
$$

We note that if $\boldsymbol{X}$ is empty or low dimensional, then one might postulate parametric models for $\theta_{\mathrm{ACO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})$, along with additional conditional mean models for $Y$ and $D$. In that case, one can test e.g. $\theta_{\mathrm{ACO}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\theta_{\mathrm{SW}, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})=0$ using standard over-identification tests, such as the Sargan-Hansen test. However, when $\boldsymbol{X}$ is moderate in dimension, then such tests may be prone both to inflated type-I error (due to nuisance model misspecification) and lack of power (relative to tests that allow for a more flexible set of alternatives). Two flexible non-parametric testing procedures are therefore described below.

# 5.2 Testing the best least squares projection 

Consider testing a generic null hypothesis $H_{0}: \xi_{P_{0}}=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$ versus $H_{1}: \xi_{P_{0}} \neq 0$. Here $\xi_{P_{0}} \in L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)$ is a function-valued parameter and it is a function of $\boldsymbol{X}$. Let $\Gamma=\{\gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta), \beta \in B\}$ denote a class of functions indexed by $\beta$, with $\gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; 0)=0$ for all $\beta$ and $B$ a subset of some linear space. Assume $\beta$ is well-identified in the sense that $\beta_{1} \neq \beta_{2}$ implies $\gamma\left(\cdot ; \beta_{1}\right) \neq \gamma\left(\cdot ; \beta_{2}\right)$. Furthermore, suppose $\Gamma$ is a closed subspace $L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)$. Then the best least squares projection of $\xi_{P_{0}}$ onto $\Gamma$ (see, e.g., Chernozhukov et al., 2018b), denoted as $\Pi\left(\xi_{P_{0}} \mid \Gamma\right)$, can be defined as

$$
\Pi\left(\xi_{P_{0}} \mid \Gamma\right)=\arg \min _{\gamma \in \Gamma}\left\|\gamma-\xi_{P_{0}}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)}
$$

The projection $\Pi\left(\xi_{P_{0}} \mid \Gamma\right)$ has the unique representation as $\gamma\left(\cdot, \beta_{P_{0}}\right)$, with $\beta_{P_{0}}$ satisfying

$$
\beta_{0}=\arg \min _{\beta \in B} \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\xi_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\gamma\left(\boldsymbol{X} ; \beta_{0}\right)\right]^{2}
$$

Under the null hypothesis $H_{0}: \xi_{P_{0}}=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$, we necessarily have $\beta_{0}=0$. Therefore, we can test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: \xi_{P_{0}}=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$ by first deriving an asymptotically normal estimator and then constructing a Wald-type test for $\beta_{0}$. Below, we will specialize our discussion to the functional parameters $\theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$ and consider testing $H_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$ in (5). Let $\beta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$ denote the projection of $\theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$ as defined in (6). Theorem 5 derives the canonical gradient for $\beta_{P}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$.

Theorem 5. Suppose $\partial \gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta) / \partial \beta$ exists and is continuous in $\beta$. Under a non-parametric model, the canonical gradient for $\beta_{P}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$ at $P_{0}$, are $\phi_{P_{0}}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3 . \phi_{P}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \phi_{P}^{(1)}:(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y) \mapsto C_{P}^{(1)} \frac{\partial \gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta)}{\partial \beta}\left|{ }_{\beta=\beta_{P}^{(1)}}\left[D_{P}^{(1)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)-D_{P}^{(2)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)+\theta_{P}^{(1)}(\boldsymbol{x})-\gamma\left(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta_{P}^{(1)}\right)\right]\right. \\
& \left.\phi_{P}^{(2)}:(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y) \mapsto C_{P}^{(2)} \frac{\partial \gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta)}{\partial \beta}\right|_{\beta=\beta_{P}^{(2)}}\left[D_{P}^{(1)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)-D_{P}^{(3)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)+\theta_{P}^{(2)}(\boldsymbol{x})-\gamma\left(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta_{P}^{(2)}\right)\right] \\
& \left.\phi_{P}^{(3)}:(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y) \mapsto C_{P}^{(3)} \frac{\partial \gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta)}{\partial \beta}\right|_{\beta=\beta_{P}^{(3)}}\left[D_{P}^{(2)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)-D_{P}^{(3)}(z, \boldsymbol{x}, d, y)+\theta_{P}^{(3)}(\boldsymbol{x})-\gamma\left(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta_{P}^{(3)}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_{P}^{(j)}$ are constants, and the expressions of $D_{P}^{(1)}, D_{P}^{(2)}$, and $D_{P}^{(3)}$ can be found in the Supplemental Material S2.9.

Analogous to the development in Section 4.3, we estimate $\beta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$ based on estimating

equations with nuisance functions estimated via flexible non-parametric methods and cross-fitting. Below, we focus on $\gamma(\boldsymbol{x} ; \beta)=\boldsymbol{x}^{T} \beta$. In this case, $\beta_{P}^{(j)}$ admits the following equivalent form:

$$
\beta_{P}^{(j)}=\left(\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{X}^{T}\right]\right)^{-1} \mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\boldsymbol{X} \theta_{P}^{(j)}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]
$$

For each $\beta_{P}^{(j)}$, our proposed test statistics can then be constructed analogously as described in Section 4.3 based on the following steps:

Step I: For each $k \in[K]$, construct the estimating equation-based estimator $\widehat{\beta}_{e e, k}^{(j)}$, where the estimating equation is defined based on the canonical gradient $\phi_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$;

Step II: Construct the cross-fitted estimating equation-based estimator $\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}=\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \widehat{\beta}_{e e, k}^{(j)}$.
Step III: Estimate the asymptotic variance $\widehat{\Sigma}^{(j)}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{K} n_{k} \mathbb{P}_{n, k}\left\{\phi^{(j)} \widehat{P}_{P_{n, k}} \phi_{P_{n, k}}^{(j)}\right\}$;
Step IV: Construct the test statistic $W^{(j)}=\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j), T} \widehat{\Sigma}^{(j),-1} \widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}$ and define the test:

$$
T_{\text {Wald }, \alpha}^{(j)}=\mathbb{1}\left\{W^{(j)}>\chi_{1-\alpha}^{2}\left(d_{\boldsymbol{x}}\right)\right\}
$$

where $d_{\boldsymbol{x}}$ is the dimension of $\boldsymbol{x}$, and $\chi_{1-\alpha}^{2}\left(d_{\boldsymbol{x}}\right)$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile for Chi-squared distribution with $d_{\boldsymbol{x}}$ degrees of freedom .

Theorem 6 establishes the properties of $\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}$ and the test $T_{\text {Wald, }}^{(j)}$.

Theorem 6. Under regularity conditions specified in Supplemental Material S2.10, for $j=1,2,3$,

1. Estimator $\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}$ is consistent and asymptotically normal, with its asymptotic variance achieving the efficiency bound:

$$
\sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}-\beta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}\right) \rightsquigarrow \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\phi_{P_{0}}^{(j) T} \phi_{P_{0}}^{(j)}\right]\right)
$$

2. The test $T_{\text {Wald }, \alpha}^{(j)}$ is an asymptotically size- $\alpha$ test.

Remark 4 (One-step estimator). Similar to estimating $S W A T E_{P_{0}}$, one may also construct a onestep estimator for $\beta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$. When $\gamma(\boldsymbol{X} ; \beta)$ is linear in $\boldsymbol{X}$, one-step estimators of $\beta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$ are equivalent to estimating equation-based estimators.

Remark 5. Three statistical tests, each based on $\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$, have different power under different scenarios, as we will explore in Section 6.2. One may also combine any two or all three tests and perform a joint test based on the asymptotic joint distribution of $\left(\widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(1)}, \widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(2)}, \widehat{\beta}_{e e}^{(3)}\right)$.

# 5.3 Non-parametric $L^{p}$ norm-based test 

Next, we describe a class of non-parametric $L^{p}$ norm-based tests motivated by Westling (2022). Again, we consider testing a null hypothesis $H_{0}: \xi_{P_{0}}=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$ versus $H_{1}: \xi_{P_{0}} \neq 0$, where $\xi_{P_{0}} \in L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)$ is a function of $\boldsymbol{X}$. Suppose $\boldsymbol{X}=\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \boldsymbol{X}_{2}\right)$, where the marginal distribution of $\boldsymbol{X}_{1}$ is absolutely continuous to the counting measure, and the marginal distribution of $\boldsymbol{X}_{2}$ is absolutely continuous to the Lebesgue measure. Let $\left\|\xi_{P_{0}}\right\|_{P_{0}, p}=\left(\int\left|\xi_{P_{0}}\right|^{p} d P_{0}\right)^{1 / p}$ for $p \geq 1$, and $\left\|\xi_{P_{0}}\right\|_{P_{0}, \infty}=\sup _{\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{X}} \xi(\boldsymbol{x})$. Let the support of $\boldsymbol{X}=\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \boldsymbol{X}_{2}\right)$ be $\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1} \times \mathcal{X}_{2} \subset \mathbb{R}^{d_{1}} \times \mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}$. Let $1_{c}(x)=1\left\{x \in\left(-\infty, c_{1}\right] \times \ldots \times\left(-\infty, c_{d_{1}}\right] \times \ldots \times\left(-\infty, c_{d_{1}+d_{2}}\right]\right\}$. The construction of the $L^{p}$ norm-based tests is based on the following technical lemma.

Lemma 1. The following statements are equivalent: (i). $\theta_{P_{0}}(x)=0$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}_{1} \times \mathcal{X}_{2}$. (ii). $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c):=\int \xi_{P_{0}}(x) 1_{c}(x) d P_{0}(x)=0$ for all $c \in \mathcal{X}$. (iii). $\left\|\Omega_{P_{0}}\right\|_{P_{0}, p}=0$ for $p \geq 1$ or $p=\infty$.

Therefore, testing the null hypothesis $\xi_{P_{0}}(x)=0$ a.s. $P_{0}$ is equivalent to testing the null hypothesis that $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)=0$ for any $c \in \mathcal{X}$. One advantage of constructing a test based on $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)$ is that $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)$ is $\sqrt{n}$-estimable for any fixed $c$ without further parametric assumptions. On the contrary, even when all the nuisance parameters and potential outcomes are known, $\theta_{P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{x})$ is not generally $\sqrt{n}$-estimable.

To construct a test, we first construct a RAL estimator of $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)$ for each fixed $c$, denoted as $\widehat{\Omega}(c)$. Similar to the estimation procedure developed in Section 5.2, we may construct a crossfitted, estimating equation-based estimator or a one-step estimator based on the efficient influence function of $\Omega_{P}(c)$ at $P_{0}$ for any fixed $c$. Suppose $\widehat{\Omega}(c)$ admits the following asymptotic expansion:

$$
\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)=\mathbb{P}_{n} D_{P_{0}}^{*}(c)+r_{n}(c)
$$

where $D_{P_{0}}^{*}(c)$ is the canonical gradient of $\Omega_{P}(c)$ at $P_{0}$. If we further have $\sup _{c \in \mathcal{X}}\left|r_{n}(c)\right|=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)$ and $\left\{D_{P_{0}}^{*}(c), c \in \mathcal{X}\right\}$ is $P_{0}-$ Donsker, then the stochastic process $\mathbb{H}_{n}:=\left\{\sqrt{n}\left[\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right]: c \in \mathcal{X}\right\}$ converges weakly in $l^{\infty}(\mathcal{X})$ to a tight, mean-zero Gaussian process $\mathbb{H}$, with covariance function

$\Sigma(s, t)=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D_{P_{0}}^{*}(s) D_{P_{0}}^{*}(t)\right]$, where $(s, t) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}$. Then by the continuous mapping theorem, $\left\|\sqrt{n}\left\{\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right\}\right\|_{P_{0}, p} \rightharpoonup\left\|\mathbb{H}\right\|_{P_{0}, p}$ for $p \geq 1$ or $p=\infty$. In practice, one may replace $\|\sqrt{n}\left\{\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\right.$ $\left.\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right\}\|_{\text {P }_{0}, p}$ with $\left\|\sqrt{n}\left\{\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right\}\right\|_{P_{n}, p}$ for $p \geq 1$ or $p=\infty$, where $\|\sqrt{n}\left\{\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right\}\|_{P_{n}, \infty}=$ $\sup _{c \in \mathcal{X}_{n}}\left|\sqrt{n}\left\{\widehat{\Omega}(c)-\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)\right\}\right|$ when $p=\infty, \mathcal{X}_{n}=\left\{\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{X}_{n}\right\}$. To simulate the $\alpha$-th quantile of $\|\mathbb{H}\|_{P_{n}, p}$, one may (i) simulate a mean-zero Gaussian process $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}_{n}$ with covariance function equal to the sample covariance function $\Sigma_{n}(s, t)=\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{P}_{n, k}\left\{D_{\widehat{P}_{n, k}}^{*}(s) D_{\widehat{P}_{n, k}}^{*}(t)\right\}$; (ii) simulate the $1-\alpha$-th quantile of $\left\|\widehat{\mathbb{H}}_{n}(c)\right\|_{P_{n}, p}$, denoted as $Q_{n, \alpha}$; and (iii) construct the test by comparing $Q_{n, \alpha}$ to $\|\sqrt{n} \widehat{\Omega}(c)\|_{P_{n}, p}$ since $\Omega_{P_{0}}(c)$ equals 0 under the null.

For $j=1,2,3$, let $\xi_{P_{0}}$ be $\theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}$, and define $\Omega_{P_{0}}^{(j)}(c):=\int \theta_{P_{0}}^{(j)}(x) 1_{c}(x) d P_{0}(x)$. Proposition 6 derives the canonical gradient for $\Omega_{P}^{(j)}(c)$.

Proposition 6. The canonical gradient for $\Omega_{P}^{(j)}(c)$ at $P_{0}$ is $D_{P_{0}}^{(j) *}(c)$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D_{P}^{(1) *}(c): o \mapsto D_{P}^{(1)}(z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-D_{P}^{(2)}(g, z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)+\theta_{P}^{(1)}(x) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-\Omega_{P}^{(1)}(c) \\
& D_{P}^{(2) *}(c): o \mapsto D_{P}^{(1)}(z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-D_{P}^{(3)}(g, z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)+\theta_{P}^{(2)}(x) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-\Omega_{P}^{(2)}(c) \\
& D_{P}^{(3) *}(c): o \mapsto D_{P}^{(2)}(z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-D_{P}^{(3)}(g, z, x, d, y) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)+\theta_{P}^{(3)}(x) \mathbb{1}_{c}(x)-\Omega_{P}^{(3)}(c)
\end{aligned}
$$

For each $j \in\{1,2,3\}$ and any fixed $c$, the proposed estimating equation-based estimator $\widehat{\Omega}_{e e}^{(j)}(c)$ of $\Omega_{P_{0}}^{(j)}(c)$, which is equivalent to the one-step estimator, can then be constructed as follows:

Step I: For each $k \in[K]$, construct the cross-fitted, estimating equation estimator $\widehat{\Omega}_{e e, k}^{(j)}(c)=$ $\Omega_{\widehat{P}_{k}}^{(j)}(c)+\mathbb{P}_{n, k} D_{\widehat{P}_{k}}^{(j) *}(c) ;$

Step II: Construct the final cross-fitted estimating equation estimator as $\widehat{\Omega}_{e e}^{(j)}(c)=\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{\Omega}_{e e, k}^{(j)}(c)$. We summarize our proposed asymptotically size- $\alpha$ test below:

Step I: For each $k \in[K]$ and a fixed $c$, construct the cross-fitted, estimating equation-based estimator $\widehat{\Omega}_{e e}^{(j)}(c)$.

Step II: Define $\mathcal{X}_{n}=\left\{\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{X}_{n}\right\}$. Let $Q_{n, \alpha}^{(j)}$ be the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\left\|\widehat{\mathbb{H}}_{n}^{(j)}\right\|_{P_{n}, p}$, where $\left(\widehat{\mathbb{H}}_{n}^{(j)}\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{1}\right), \ldots, \widehat{\mathbb{H}}_{n}^{(j)}\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{n}\right)\right)$ is distributed to a mean-zero multivariate normal distribution with $(s, t)-t h$ element of covariance matrix given by $\Sigma_{n}^{(j)}\left(X_{s}, X_{j}\right)$, where $\Sigma_{n}^{(j)}(s, t)=\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{P}_{n, k}$ $\left\{D_{\widehat{P}_{n, k}}^{(j) *}(s) D_{\widehat{P}_{n, k}}^{(j) *}(t)\right\}, 1 \leq s, t \leq n$, conditional on data $\left(O_{1}, \ldots, O_{n}\right)$.

Step III: Define the test: $T_{n p, \alpha}^{(j)}=\mathbb{1}\left\{\sup _{i}\left\|\widehat{\Omega}^{(j)}\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{i}\right)\right\|_{P_{n}, p}>Q_{n, \alpha}^{(j)}\right\}$.

Theorem 7 summarizes the properties of the proposed test $T_{n p, \alpha}^{(j)}$.

Theorem 7. Under regularity conditions specified in Supplemental Material S2.13,

1. $T_{n p, \alpha}^{(j)}$ is an asymptotically size $\alpha$ test.
2. The asymptotic power of $T_{n p, \alpha}^{(j)}$ is 1 .
3. $T_{n p, \alpha}^{(j)}$ has non-trivial power under local alternative distributions $P_{n}$ :

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \int\left[n^{1 / 2}\left(d P_{n}^{1 / 2}-d P_{0}^{1 / 2}\right)-\frac{1}{2} h d P_{0}^{1 / 2}\right]=0
$$

where $h$ is a score function with $P_{0} h=0$ and $P_{0} h^{2}<\infty$.

Remark 6 (Choice of $p$ ). Two choices of $p$ are often adopted in the literature: $p=2$, corresponding to the Cramer-von Mises-type test, and $p=\infty$, corresponding to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov-type test.

Remark 7 (Computation cost). Unlike $T_{\text {Wald }}^{(j)}$, the proposed non-parametric $L^{p}$ norm-based tests are computationally challenging when the dimension of $\boldsymbol{X}$ is moderately large, because the procedure requires simulating a Gaussian process indexed by a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$. On the other hand, the computation cost of the best least squares projection-based test is essentially agnostic to the dimension of $\boldsymbol{X}$.

# 6 Simulation study 

We have three goals in this simulation study. First, we investigate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators for SWATE. Second, we investigate the level of each projection-based test for the null hypotheses $H_{0}^{(j)}$. Because test $T_{\text {Wald }, \alpha}^{(j)}$ developed for $H_{0}^{(j)}, j=1,2,3$, can each be used to test the same null hypothesis Assumption $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{i})$ or $\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{ii})$, we also compare their power. Third, we compare the level and power of the projection-based test and two non-parametric $L^{p}$ norm-based tests.

# 6.1 Estimation of SWATE 

We generate datasets according to the following factorial design:
Sample sizes: $N=1000,2000,5000$ and 10000 .
Baseline covariates: We consider a eight-dimensional covariate $\boldsymbol{X}=\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \boldsymbol{X}_{2}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{X}_{8}\right)$, where $\left(\boldsymbol{X}_{1}, \boldsymbol{X}_{2}, \boldsymbol{X}_{3}\right) \sim \mathcal{M} \mathcal{V} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, with $\mu=(0,1,-0.5), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\left(\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0.2 & -0.3 \\ 0.2 & 1 & 0.1 \\ -0.3 & 0.1 & 1\end{array}\right)$, and truncated at -4 and $4, \boldsymbol{X}_{4}, \boldsymbol{X}_{5}, \boldsymbol{X}_{6} \sim$ Bernoulli( 0.5$), \boldsymbol{X}_{7} \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(-3,3)$, and $\boldsymbol{X}_{8} \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(4,0.5)$.
Instrumental variable: We generate a binary stratification variable $G \in\{a, b\}$ according to $P(G=a)=1-\operatorname{expit}\left(1+0.2 X_{1}-0.1 X_{2}+0.3 X_{3}\right)$ and $P(G=b)=1-P(G=a)$, where $\operatorname{expit}(x)=\exp (x) /(1+\exp (x))$ is the inverse of the logit function. Conditioning on $G=a$ or $b$, we then generate a binary IV $Z \in\left\{0_{a}, 1_{a}\right\}$ when $G=a$ and $Z \in\left\{0_{b}, 1_{b}\right\}$ when $G=b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left(Z=1_{a} \mid G=a\right)=\operatorname{expit}\left(1+0.5 X_{1}-X_{2}+0.7 X_{3}\right) \\
& P\left(Z=1_{b} \mid G=b\right)=\operatorname{expit}\left(0.5+0.6 X_{1}+0.3 X_{2}+0.4 X_{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

According to this data generating process, the IV assignment is dependent on observed covariates and different for $G=a$ or $b$.

Unmeasured confounder: We generate an unmeasured confounder $U \sim \mathcal{N}(0,0.6)$. Scalar representation of unobserved confounding is widely adopted in the literature and referred to as a "principal unobserved covariate" (Rosenbaum and Rubin, 2023).

Principal stratum: The principal stratum status of participant $i$, denoted as $S_{i}$, is generated via a multinomial distribution: $P\left(S_{i}=j\right)=\frac{g_{j}}{\sum_{j} g_{j}}, j \in\{\mathrm{ANT}, \mathrm{SW} 1, \mathrm{SW} 2, \mathrm{AT}-\mathrm{NT}, \mathrm{ACO}, \mathrm{NT}-\mathrm{AT}, \mathrm{AAT}\}$. The principal strata $S W 1$ and $S W 2$ correspond to participants who convert from always-takers or never-takers to compliers, respectively. We specify $g_{j}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
g_{A N T}=\exp \left(1-X_{2}+0.7 X_{3}+0.3 U\right), & g_{S W 1}=\exp \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\left(X_{1}+2 X_{2}-X_{3}\right)+\alpha_{3} U\right) \\
g_{S W 2}=\exp \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\left(-X_{1}-2 X_{2}\right)+\alpha_{3} U\right), & g_{A T-N T}=\exp \left(1+0.5 X_{1}+X_{2}+0.5 X_{3}+0.5 U\right) \\
g_{A C O}=\exp \left(1+0.8 X_{1}-2 X_{2}-2 X_{3}+0.5 U\right), & g_{N T-A T}=\exp \left(1-0.5 X_{1}-1 X_{2}-0.5 X_{3}-0.5 U\right) \\
g_{A A T}=\exp \left(1+2 X_{1}+2 X_{3}-U\right), &
\end{array}
$$

where parameters $\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}\right)$ control the proportions of switchers. We consider the following 4

choices of $\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}\right):(-0.2,0.1,0.0005),(0.5,0.2,0.05),(0.3,0.5,0.1)$, and $(1,1,1)$, corresponding to $11 \%, 22 \%, 32 \%$, and $66 \%$ switchers in the population, respectively.

Treatment received: Treatment received $D$ is determined by $Z$ and $S$.
Outcome: We consider two sets of data generating processes for potential outcomes: For a continuous outcome, we generate $Y(0)=1+X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+U+\epsilon$ and $Y(1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y(1)= & \mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{ANT} \text { or AAT }\right\} \cdot\left(1+X_{1}+2 X_{2}+2 X_{3}+X_{4}+U\right) \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{AT}-\mathrm{NT} \text { or NT-AT }\right\} \cdot\left(1+X_{1}+X_{2}+2 X_{3}+X_{4}+U\right) \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{SWI}\right\} \cdot\left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2} X_{1}+2 X_{2}+\beta_{3} X_{3}+X_{4}+U\right) \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{ACO}\right\} \cdot\left(1+X_{1}+2 X_{2}+0.2 X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+U\right)+\epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \beta_{3}\right)=(2,2,2)$ or $(4,4,4)$ control the effect size of SWATE, and $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.
For a binary outcome, potential outcomes are generated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y(0)=1) & =\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{ANT} \text { or AAT }\right\} \cdot \operatorname{expit}\left(1+X_{1}+2 X_{2}+2 X_{3}+X_{4}+X_{5}-X_{6}-X_{7}+X_{8}+U\right) \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{AT}-\mathrm{NT} \text { or NT-AT }\right\} \cdot \operatorname{expit}\left\{1+X_{1}+X_{2}+2 X_{3}+X_{4}+X_{5}-X_{6}-X_{7}+X_{8}+U\right\} \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{SWI}\right\} \cdot \operatorname{expit}\left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2} X_{1}+2 X_{2}+X_{3}+\beta_{3} X_{6}-X_{7}+2 X_{8}+U\right) \\
& +\mathbb{1}\left\{S=\mathrm{ACO}\right\} \cdot \operatorname{expit}\left(1+X_{1}+2 X_{2}+0.2 X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+X_{5}-X_{6}-X_{7}+X_{8}+U\right) \\
P(Y(1)=1) & =\operatorname{expit}\left(1+X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+U\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \beta_{3}\right)=(0,1,-1)$ or $(0,2,-3)$ control the size of SWATE. For a binary outcome, SWATE is the causal risk difference (RD) among switchers. The ground truth SWATE was calculated using Monte Carlo methods based on a simulated dataset of size 1 million.

According to the above data generating processes, nuisance functions in the canonical gradient do not have explicit forms. For each simulated dataset, we constructed the proposed estimator $\widehat{\psi}_{e e}$ with all nuisance functions estimated using the R (R Core Team, 2013) package SuperLearner (Van der Laan et al., 2007). Specifically, we included the random forest and generalized linear models in the SuperLearner library. For each of the $2 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2=48$ settings determined by the outcome type, sample size, $\left(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}\right)$ and $\left(\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \beta_{3}\right)$, we repeated the simulation 1000 times. The standard error of $\widehat{\psi}_{e e}$ was estimated based on the efficient influence function, as described in Section 4.3.

Overall, the sampling distributions appeared normal except in settings where both the proportion of switchers and the sample size are small (e.g., $n=1000$ with $11 \%$ switchers). For a fixed proportion of switchers, the sampling distributions are more concentrated around the true values as the sample size increases. Similarly, for a fixed sample size, the sampling distribution becomes more concentrated around the true values as the proportion of switchers increases. Table 2 further reports the bias, relative bias and coverage probability for different settings. We have observed come consistent trends. First, when the proportion of switchers is small, say $11 \%$, then a large sample size (e.g., $n=10000$ ) is needed for the proposed estimator to achieve a small relative bias and its $95 \%$ confidence intervals to achieve nominal coverage.
