# 8 Discussion 

In this work, we systematically study the problem with a pair of nested instrumental variables. We show that the switcher average treatment effect, or SWATE, can be non-parametrically identified under a novel nested IV assumption and develop an efficient-influence-function-based estimator for it. We also develop a projection-based test and a non-parametric test that formally assess the effect-homogeneity-type assumptions under our proposed nested IV framework.

Our paper contributes to the discussion on violation of the SUTVA (Imbens and Rubin, 2015). In the PLCO trial and similar multicentre or multiphasic trials, there may exist multiple versions of encouragement for treatment uptake, a subtlety that could be easily overlooked. In the presence of multiple versions of an IV, the usual intention-to-treat effect and the Wald estimand do not have their usual causal interpretations. The differentiation between two distinct versions of IV gives us an opportunity to study additional principal causal effects induced by the nested IV structure and test for effect heterogeneity. Interestingly, our identified conditional switcher average treatment has a similar form as the conditional ATE under the so-called instrumented difference-in-differences setting (Ye et al., 2023); however, the SWATE estimand proposed in this article is obtained by integrating over the covariate distribution among switchers, while Ye et al.’s (2023) marginalized estimand is obtained by integrating over the covariate distribution of the entire study population. Furthermore, in our setting, the abundance of principal strata complicates the model for treatment uptake and potential outcomes; hence, the current article focused on non-parametric estimators that permit using flexible non-parametric methods for nuisance functions estimation rather the usual doubly robust estimators that require correct specification for parametric nuisance models (Rotnitzky et al., 2020).

Our methods also provide some insight into testing the equality of two function-valued parameters (Hudson et al., 2021, 2023). We provide a general framework for such testing problems by projecting the function-valued parameter to a subspace of $L^{2}(P)$. In principle, one can project the parameters onto an infinite-dimensional space; in practice, projection onto a finite dimensional space suffices for type-I error control and appears to have good finite-sample power. Moreover, compared to a non-parametric test, e.g., our generalization of Westling (2022), a projection-based test is computationally more efficient and easier to implement when covariates are of moderate to high dimension.

Switcher average treatment effect is an example of the principal treatment effect. Principal effects are sometimes criticized for not being the most relevant for clinical decision making as they are concerned about the effects among unidentified subgroups; however, SWATE is clinically meaningful when researchers are interested in the practical utility of improving the compliance: a small SWATE effectively conveys the message that the marginal gain of improving compliance may be low for a target population, while a large SWATE could be an encouraging marching order for implementation scientists to investigate how to improve treatment adherence which has potential to translate to improved clinical outcomes.

The assumption of mean exchangeability over $G$, which may represent time (as in the analysis of the policy shift in Henry Ford Health System in Section 7) or different clinical sites (as in the integrated analysis of multicentre trial data in Supplemental Material S6.1), is crucial. In the case of a sudden policy shift, an unconditional version of mean exchangeability may be sufficient, as $G$ is likely to be exogenous. However, in the integrated clinical trial analysis, differences in trial participation between the University of Colorado and Henry Ford Health System could influence the effect of the IV on treatment uptake, or even the effect of treatment uptake on clinical outcomes. Therefore, conditioning on observed covariates is necessary to reduce the risk of residual confounding.

In general, even a valid IV cannot point identify the marginal and conditional treatment effects without restricting heterogeneity in some sense. Since it was an aim of this work to investigate treatment effect heterogeneity with non-compliance, we did not impose these type of restrictions. It is an interesting question for future work whether alternative non-principal interpretations of the ACOATE and SWATE functionals exist, without imposing homogeneity. In this article, we focus

on identifying and estimating the SWATE using individual-level data.

# S1 Connection to the literature on multiple instrumental variables
### S1.1 Monotonicity assumptions

An alternative approach for defining the potential outcomes is by using a vector-valued instrumental variable $\left(Z^{*}, G\right)$, where $Z^{*} \in\{0,1\}$ indicates whether an individual is assigned to the treatment group or the control group, and $G$ is the stratification variable, taking values in $\{a, b\}$. For $g \in\{a, b\}$, one may alternatively write $D\left(Z=1_{g}\right)$ as $D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=g\right)$ and $D\left(Z=0_{g}\right)$ as $D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=g\right)$. Under this vector-valued IV formulation, we may compare our partial monotonicity assumption (denoted as PM) to (1) the partial monotonicity assumption in Mogstad et al. (2021) (denoted as PM2); (2) the limited monotonicity assumption in Hoff et al. (2024) (denoted as LiM); and (3) the vector monotonicity assumption in Goff (2024) (denoted as VM), when both $Z^{*}$ and $G$ are binary.

Below, we first rewrite each monotonicity assumption using the notation in the current manuscript:
Definition S1. 1. $(\boldsymbol{P M}) . D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=g\right) \geq D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=g\right)$ for $g \in\{a, b\}$.
2. (PM2). $D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=g\right) \geq D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=g\right)$ for $g \in\{a, b\}$ and $D\left(Z^{*}=z, G=a\right) \geq$ $D\left(Z^{*}=z, G=b\right)$ for $z \in\{0,1\}$.
3. $(\boldsymbol{L i M}) . D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right) \geq D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)$.
4. $(\boldsymbol{V M}) . D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=g\right) \geq D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=g\right)$ or and $D\left(Z^{*}=z, G=a\right) \geq D\left(Z^{*}=z, G=b\right)$ for $z \in\{0,1\}$.

For the definition of PM2, we imposed similar direction constraint as equation (7) of Mogstad et al. (2021). Under the setting considered in this article, we have the following relationship among these 4 definitions:

1. PM2 and VM are equivalent.
2. PM2 implies PM and LiM.

3. PM and LiM don't imply each other.

Importantly, PM, PM2 (VM) and LiM imply the existence of different principal strata, which is summarized in Table S1. LiM is the weakest assumption and implies 12 out of 16 possible principal strata. PM2 (VM) implies 6 principal strata, which is also a proper subset of the 9 principal strata PM implies. PM, together with the key nested IV assumption considered in the current article, implies 7 principal strata, including Always-Taker-Never-Taker (AT-NT) and Always-TakerComplier (a particular type of Switcher), that do not exist under PM2 (VM). Complier-AlwaysTaker, which exists under PM2 (VM), no longer exists under PM + Nested IV.

# S1.2 Related estimands 

Goff (2024) introduced a new principal treatment effect called combined compliers local average treatment effect (CC-LATE). The combined compliers (denoted as $S=C C$ ) is defined as the subgroup with $D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)=0$ and $D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right)=1$. Under regularity conditions, the CC-LATE, defined as

$$
\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{CC}]
$$

can be identified via the following identification formula:

$$
\text { CC-LATE }=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1, G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0, G=a\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1, G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0, G=a\right]}
$$

Goff (2024) defined the following four principal strata:

1. $Z^{*}$ complier, defined as participants with $\left(D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=b\right)=\right.$ $\left.0, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=a\right)=1, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right)=1\right)$ and denoted as $S=Z^{*}$-complier;
2. $G$-complier, defined as participants with $\left(D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=b\right)=\right.$ $\left.1, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right)=1\right)$ and denoted as $S=G$-complier;
3. Reluctant compliers, defined as participants with $\left(D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=\right.\right.$ $b)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right)=1$ ) and denoted as $S=\mathrm{RC}$;
4. Eager compliers, defined as participants with $\left(D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=a\right)=0, D\left(Z^{*}=0, G=b\right)=\right.$ $\left.1, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=a\right)=1, D\left(Z^{*}=1, G=b\right)=1\right)$ and denoted as $S=\mathrm{EC}$.

Intuitively, $Z^{*}$-compliers refers to those whose compliance behavior is only determined by $Z^{*}$; $G$-compliers refer to those whose compliance behavior is only determined by $G$. The average treatment effects among those four principal strata can be identified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0)\left|S=Z^{*}\right. \text {-compliers }]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0\right]} \\
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0)\left|S=G \text {-compliers }\right]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y \mid G=a]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid G=a\right]} \\
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{RC}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1, G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0 \text { or } G=a\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1, G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0 \text { or } G=a\right]} \\
& \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y(D=1)-Y(D=0) \mid S=\mathrm{EC}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=1 \text { or } G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z^{*}=0, G=a\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=1 \text { or } G=b\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[D \mid Z^{*}=0, G=a\right]}
\end{aligned}
$$

All of the above causal estimands can be identified by Wald-type identification formula.

= & P\left\{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\} \frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\left[l-\mu_{L, z}\right]+\mu_{L, z}\right\}+P\left\{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{z}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\right)\left(\mu_{L, z}-\bar{\mu}_{L, z}\right)\right\} \\
& +P\left\{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\} \frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\left(\bar{\mu}_{L, z}-\mu_{L, z}\right)-\left(\bar{\mu}_{L, z}-\mu_{L, z}\right)\right\}+P\left\{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{z}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\right)\left(y-\mu_{L, z}\right)\right\} \\
= & P \mu_{L, z}+P\left\{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{z}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\right)\left(\mu_{L, z}-\bar{\mu}_{L, z}\right)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Plug this into $R(\bar{P}, P)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R(\bar{P}, P) \\
= & \Psi_{S W, \bar{P}}-\Psi_{S W, P}+P D_{\bar{P}} \\
= & \frac{1}{\bar{\omega}_{2}}\left\{P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{1_{b}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{1_{b}}}\right)\left(\mu_{Y, 1_{b}}-\bar{\mu}_{Y, 1_{b}}\right)\right]-P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{0_{b}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{0_{b}}}\right)\left(\mu_{Y, 0_{b}}-\bar{\mu}_{Y, 0_{b}}\right)\right]\right. \\
& \left.-P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{a}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{1_{a}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{1_{a}}}\right)\left(\mu_{Y, 1_{a}}-\bar{\mu}_{Y, 1_{a}}\right)\right]+P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{a}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{0_{a}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{0_{a}}}\right)\left(\mu_{Y, 0_{a}}-\bar{\mu}_{Y, 0_{a}}\right)\right]\right\} \\
& -\frac{\bar{\omega}_{1}}{\bar{\omega}_{2}^{2}}\left\{P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{1_{b}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{1_{b}}}\right)\left(\mu_{D, 1_{b}}-\bar{\mu}_{D, 1_{b}}\right)\right]-P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{0_{b}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{0_{b}}}\right)\left(\mu_{D, 0_{b}}-\bar{\mu}_{D, 0_{b}}\right)\right]\right. \\
& \left.-P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{a}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{1_{a}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{1_{a}}}\right)\left(\mu_{D, 1_{a}}-\bar{\mu}_{D, 1_{a}}\right)\right]+P\left[\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{a}\right\}\left(\frac{1}{\bar{\pi}_{0_{a}}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{0_{a}}}\right)\left(\mu_{D, 0_{a}}-\bar{\mu}_{D, 0_{a}}\right)\right]\right\} \\
& +\frac{1}{\bar{\omega}_{2}^{2}}\left(\omega_{2}-\bar{\omega}_{2}\right)\left(\bar{\omega}_{1}-\omega_{1}\right)+\frac{\omega_{1}}{\bar{\omega}_{2}^{2} \omega_{2}}\left(\omega_{2}-\bar{\omega}_{2}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then for $k=1, \ldots, K$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\psi}_{o s, k}-\Psi_{S W, P_{0}} \\
= & \Psi_{S W, \hat{P}_{n, k}}+\mathbb{P}_{n, k} D_{\hat{P}_{n}}-\Psi_{S W, P_{0}} \\
= & \left(\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right) D_{P_{0}}+\left(\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right)\left(D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right)+R\left(\hat{P}_{n, k}, P_{0}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

We will show that $\sqrt{n} R\left(\hat{P}_{n, k}, P_{0}\right)=o_{p}(1)$. Now we define new notations

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \hat{\pi}_{z, k}(x)=\hat{P}_{n, k}(Z=z \mid X=x), \pi_{0, z}(x)=P_{0}(Z=z \mid X=x) \\
& \hat{\mu}_{Y, z, k}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}[Y \mid Z=z, X=x], \mu_{0, Y, z}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[Y \mid Z=z, X=x] \\
& \hat{\mu}_{D, z, k}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}[D \mid Z=z, X=x], \mu_{0, D, z}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[D \mid Z=z, X=x] \\
& \hat{\omega}_{1, k}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}\left[\delta_{b, \hat{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\delta_{a, \hat{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right], \omega_{0,1}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\delta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\delta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right] \\
& \hat{\omega}_{2, k}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}\left[\eta_{b, \hat{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, \hat{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right], \omega_{0,2}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\eta_{b, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\eta_{a, P_{0}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Then with probability approaching one, we know there exists a constant $C$ such that

$$
\left|\frac{1}{\hat{\omega}_{2, k}}\right| \leq C,\left|\frac{1}{\hat{\omega}_{2, k}^{2}}\right| \leq C,\left|\frac{\hat{\omega}_{1, k}}{\hat{\omega}_{2, k}^{2}}\right| \leq C,\left|\frac{\hat{\omega}_{1, k}}{\hat{\omega}_{2, k}^{2} \omega_{0,2}}\right| \leq C
$$

Under our assumptions for nuisance parameter estimation, we have

$$
P_{0}\left[\mathbb{1}\{z=z\}\left(\frac{1}{\hat{\pi}_{z, k}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\right)\left(\mu_{B, z}-\hat{\mu}_{B, z, k}\right)\right] \leq C\left\|\frac{1}{\hat{\pi}_{z, k}}-\frac{1}{\pi_{z}}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)}\left\|\mu_{B, z}-\hat{\mu}_{B, z, k}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(P_{0}\right)}=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)
$$

for $z \in\left\{1_{b}, 0_{b}, 1_{a}, 0_{a}\right\}$. Similarly, by the fact we used cross-fitting and Holder's inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left|\omega_{0,2}-\hat{\omega}_{2, k}\right|\left|\omega_{0,1}-\hat{\omega}_{1, k}\right|=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right) \\
& \left|\omega_{0,2}-\hat{\omega}_{2, k}\right|^{2}=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have proved that $R\left(\hat{P}_{n, k}, P_{0}\right)=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)$.
Now we discuss how to handle $\left(\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right)\left(D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right)$. Since we used cross-fitting, we have for fixed $t>0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{0}\left\{\left|\left[\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right]\left[D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right]\right|>(n / K)^{-1 / 2} t \mid k \text {-th subsample }\right\} \\
\leq & \min \left\{1, \frac{\operatorname{Var}\left\{\left[D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right] \mid k \text {-th subsample }\right\}}{t^{2}}\right\} \\
= & \min \left\{1, \frac{P_{0}\left\{\left[D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right]^{2} \mid k \text {-th subsample }\right\}}{t^{2}}\right\} \\
= & \min \left\{1, \frac{P_{0}\left[D_{\hat{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right]^{2}}{t^{2}}\right\} \\
= & \min \left\{1, o_{p}(1)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking an expectation of both sides and applying the dominated convergence theorem shows

that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{0}\left\{\left|\left[\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right]\left[D_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right]\right|>(n / K)^{-1 / 2} t\right\} \\
= & E\left[\min 1, o_{p}(1)\right] \\
& \rightarrow 0
\end{aligned}
$$

As $t>0$ was arbitrary, we have

$$
\left(\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right)\left(D_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}-D_{P_{0}}\right)=o_{p}\left(n^{-1 / 2}\right)
$$

To sum up,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{n}\left(\hat{\psi}_{o s}-\Psi_{S W, P_{0}}\right) \\
= & \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\hat{\psi}_{o s, k}-\Psi_{S W, P_{0}}\right)\right) \\
= & \sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\mathbb{P}_{n, k}-P_{0}\right) D_{P_{0}}\right)+o_{p}(1) \\
= & \sqrt{n}\left(\mathbb{P}_{n}-P_{0}\right) D_{P_{0}} \\
\leadsto & N\left(0, P_{0} D_{P_{0}}^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the last line holds if we further assume $P_{0} D_{P_{0}}^{2}<\infty$.
For $\hat{\psi}_{e e}$, we notice that

$$
\hat{\psi}_{e e, k}=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{n, k} A_{n, k}}{\mathbb{P}_{n, k} B_{n, k}}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{n, k} & =\frac{1\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=1_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}[Y \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]\right]-\frac{1\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=0_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}[Y \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]\right] \\
& -\frac{1\left\{z=1_{a}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=1_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}[Y \mid Z=1_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]\right]+\frac{1\left\{z=0_{a}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=0_{a} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}_{n, k}}[Y \mid Z=0_{a}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}]\right] \\
& +\delta_{b, \tilde{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{x})-\delta_{a, \tilde{P}_{n, k}}(\boldsymbol{x})
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_{n, k}= & \frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=1_{b}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=1_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}}\left[D \mid Z=1_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right]-\frac{\mathbb{1}\left\{z=0_{b}\right\}}{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}\left(Z=0_{b} \mid \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right)}\left[d-\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{P}_{n, k}}\left[D \mid Z=0_{b}, \boldsymbol{X}=\boldsymbol{x}\right]\right] \\

\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

& -\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z=0_{b}, X=x\right]-\frac{\mathbb{1}\left(z=0_{b}\right)}{P_{0}\left(Z=0_{b} \mid X=x\right)}\left[y-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid Z=z, X=x\right]\right] \\

\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)=x_{1} / x_{2}$, then by delta method Van der Vaart (2000), $\widehat{\psi}_{e e, k}$ should also be asymptotically linear, where the influence function should be

$$

Proof. Suppose principal ignorability holds, then by definition of principal ignorability, we have

Suppose no unmeasured common effect modifier holds, then

$$
\begin{gathered}

$$
\begin{gathered}

\end{gathered}

similarly we have

$$

$$

& \left(\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid X, Z=1_{a}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid X, Z=0_{a}\right]\right)-\left(\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid X, Z=1_{b}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[Y \mid X, Z=0_{b}\right]\right) \\

$$

abstract:
Instrumental variables (IV) are a commonly used tool to estimate causal
effects from non-randomized data. An archetype of an IV is a randomized trial
with non-compliance where the randomized treatment assignment serves as an IV
for the non-ignorable treatment received. Under a monotonicity assumption, a
valid IV non-parametrically identifies the average treatment effect among a
non-identified, latent complier subgroup, whose generalizability is often under
debate. In many studies, there could exist multiple versions of an IV, for
instance, different nudges to take the same treatment in different study sites
in a multicentre clinical trial. These different versions of an IV may result
in different compliance rates and offer a unique opportunity to study IV
estimates' generalizability. In this article, we introduce a novel nested IV
assumption and study identification of the average treatment effect among two
latent subgroups: always-compliers and switchers, who are defined based on the
joint potential treatment received under two versions of a binary IV. We derive
the efficient influence function for the SWitcher Average Treatment Effect
(SWATE) under a non-parametric model and propose efficient estimators. We then
propose formal statistical tests of the generalizability of IV estimates under
the nested IV framework. We apply the proposed method to the Prostate, Lung,
Colorectal and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial and study the causal
effect of colorectal cancer screening and its generalizability.
